Execute the scientific discovery task in the current workspace now. Do not wait for confirmation and do not stop after writing a plan.

1. Read `PublicTaskContract.md`, `ResearchObjective.md`, `DATA_GUIDE.md`, `data_manifest.json`, and `validate_output.py` completely. 2. Treat the current task and data as the only benchmark-provided scientific input for this run. entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

1	# TruthInsightBench Public Scientific Discovery Contract
2	
3	## Objective
4	
5	Use the scientific data in the current task workspace as the sole direct evidence for core findings. Independently propose, test, and report reproducible, bounded, and falsifiable scientific findings. External information that satisfies the time boundary below may support only background, methods, or alternative explanations.
6	
7	The task does not presume that any candidate relationship is true. Null effects, reverse relationships, conditional conflicts, applicability boundaries, and evidence-backed unresolved results are valid conclusions. Never assume that a relationship must exist merely because it falls within the research objective.
8	
9	## Scientific inputs visible to the Agent
10	
11	The benchmark supplies only the canonical scientific content below. A native launcher may expose the components as separate files or embed them losslessly in the platform's required single research-goal entry file. That presentation difference adds no scientific direction or evidence. A platform's native system prompt, tools, and execution framework belong to the evaluated Agent and are not benchmark hints.
12	
13	1. This public task contract.
14	2. The current task's neutral research objective.
15	3. The task-level data interpretation notes in `DATA_GUIDE.md`.
16	4. The data inventory, fields, units, analysis unit, missingness notes, license boundary, and hashes in `data_manifest.json`.
17	5. The current task's scientific data under `data/`.
18	6. The public semantic completion validator `validate_output.py`. It verifies delivery roles and traceability only and is not scientific evidence.
19	
20	Evaluator-private materials, scoring assets, other task workspaces, historical runs, historical scores, and other Agents' outputs are outside the scientific input boundary and must not be sought or used.
21	
22	## Reporting language
23	
24	Write the authoritative report and Agent-authored scientific narrative in English. Preserve raw data values, symbols, source labels, code identifiers, and file names when translation would alter the evidence or break reproducibility.
25	
26	## Evidence and time boundary
27	
28	- Workspace data are the only direct evidence for a core scientific claim.
29	- External literature search is optional. When a task specifies `T0`, an external source may be used only if it was first public strictly before `T0`, and only for background, methods, or alternative explanations.
30	- For every external source used, record a citation and stable URL or identifier plus its first-public date in the report or a linked source log. If that date cannot be verified as strictly before `T0`, do not use the source.
31	- Do not use external search to identify or reconstruct the hidden source behind the task, its authors, title, identifier, repository, exact wording, target values, or conclusions first released on or after `T0`.
32	- Do not download, substitute, or merge an external scientific dataset or precomputed task result into the evidentiary analysis. The workspace `data/` directory is the complete dataset for this task.
33	- Do not describe an unrun method, unread datum, unobserved result, or background reference as direct evidence from this task.
34	
35	## Required research actions
36	
37	1. Identify files, variables, units, independent analysis units, repeated-measure structure, and missing-data boundaries.
38	2. For each key candidate relationship, compare at least one null or simple baseline explanation and discuss additional alternatives where the data allow.
39	3. Run code that produces the core numerical evidence. File names, comments, visual impressions, and model self-reports are not executed evidence.
40	4. Apply at least one task-appropriate robustness check to each submitted finding, such as complete-unit or batch leave-out, an alternative definition, threshold sensitivity, an alternative model, or an outlier-treatment comparison.
41	5. Distinguish direct observations, data-supported inferences, mechanism interpretations, and unresolved questions.
42	6. Report failed, conflicting, or unresolved tests that materially bear on a submitted claim; do not silently discard them.
43	
44	## Finding registration
45	
46	Register 2 to 5 high-level research conclusions for scoring. A conclusion may report a supported relationship, reverse relationship, null effect, conditional conflict, applicability boundary, or evidence-backed unresolved result. The minimum of two does not mean two affirmative claims. Do not split one conclusion into synonyms or lower the evidence standard to meet the minimum.
47	
48	Make the registered set mechanically identifiable in the final report. Label each registered conclusion consecutively from 1 using a Markdown heading or bold label that begins with `Finding 1`, `Discovery 1`, or `D1` (case-insensitive), followed by the corresponding labels through the final finding. The label is only an index; the scientific content remains ordinary report prose.
49	
50	For every registered finding, state at least:
51	
52	- object and scope;
53	- relationship, direction, or boundary;
54	- core quantitative result and analysis unit;
55	- supporting analysis and result evidence, identified either by exact path or by a native artifact/task identifier that resolves to real files;
56	- robustness result;
57	- counterevidence, limitation, and alternative explanations; and
58	- an executable new observation or independent replication that could falsify or validate it.
59	
60	Supporting observations, background, limitations, and evidence rows for one finding do not automatically become additional findings.
61	
62	## Semantic delivery contract
63	
64	The benchmark standardizes the scientific functions of the output, not a shared internal directory layout. Every run must provide all five semantic roles below under `output/`:
65	
66	1. **Authoritative findings:** one non-empty root Markdown report, matched case-insensitively as `Result.md`, containing the complete set of 2 to 5 registered findings, qualifications, limitations, and validation proposals.
67	2. **Executed analysis source:** scientific code or notebooks actually used. These may appear anywhere in the Agent's native output tree.
68	3. **Inspectable result evidence:** at least one machine-readable result artifact or supporting figure. It may appear anywhere in the native output tree; no `tables/` or `figures/` directory name is prescribed.
69	4. **Reproduction trace:** either a companion reproduction document, a clearly headed reproduction or methods section linked to the analysis source, or an executed native notebook trace with source and outputs.
70	5. **Finding-to-evidence traceability:** every registered finding must resolve to real analysis and result evidence. Direct paths and unambiguous file names are valid. Native artifact IDs, task IDs, notebook-cell references, and artifact registries are equally valid when they resolve to real files.
71	
72	The root Markdown report is the sole authority for which findings are submitted for scoring. Supporting task reports, notebooks, registries, dashboards, HTML, PDF, logs, and other native process files provide evidence and provenance but cannot introduce a scored claim that is absent from the root report.
73	
74	The benchmark does not request a second Agent-authored structured restatement of the report. After the run, the evaluator generates a read-only semantic inventory that maps the five roles to real files and hashes without rewriting the Agent's conclusions.
75	
76	Preserve the platform's normal scientific-process and state files. No additional standardized process tree is required beyond the five semantic roles. Unreferenced file count, report length, and native-process complexity do not increase the scientific score.
77	
78	## Integrity and failure handling
79	
80	Do not fabricate commands, numbers, code execution, figures, references, network access, or error recovery. If one library, file, fit, or tool fails, preserve the real error and continue with an executable simpler method. If full completion is impossible, submit the completed artifacts and state the exact gap.
81

Never assume that a relationship must exist merely because it falls within the research objective.

## Scientific inputs visible to the Agent

The benchmark supplies only the canonical scientific content below. A native launcher may expose the components as separate files or embed them losslessly in the platform's required single research-goal entry file. That presentation difference adds no scientific direction or evidence. A platform's native system prompt, tools, and execution framework belong to the evaluated Agent and are not benchmark hints.

1. This public task contract.
2. The current task's neutral research objective.
3. The task-level data interpretation notes in `DATA_GUIDE.md`.
4. The data inventory, fields, units, analysis unit, missingness notes, license boundary, and hashes in `data_manifest.json`.
5. The current task's scientific data under `data/`.
6. The public semantic completion validator `validate_output.py`. It verifies delivery roles and traceability only and is not scientific evidence.

Evaluator-private materials, scoring assets, other task workspaces, historical runs, historical scores, and other Agents' outputs are outside the scientific input boundary and must not be sought or used.

## Reporting language

Write the authoritative report and Agent-authored scientific narrative in English. Preserve raw data values, symbols, source labels, code identifiers, and file names when translation would alter the evidence or break reproducibility.

## Evidence and time boundary

- Workspace data are the only direct evidence for a core scientific claim.
- External literature search is optional. When a task specifies `T0`, an external source may be used only if it was first public strictly before `T0`, and only for background, methods, or alternative explanations.
- For every external source used, record a citation and stable URL or identifier plus its first-public date in the report or a linked source log. If that date cannot be verified as strictly before `T0`, do not use the source.
- Do not use external search to identify or reconstruct the hidden source behind the task, its authors, title, identifier, repository, exact wording, target values, or conclusions first released on or after `T0`.
- Do not download, substitute, or merge an external scientific dataset or precomputed task result into the evidentiary analysis. The workspace `data/` directory is the complete dataset for this task.
- Do not describe an unrun method, unread datum, unobserved result, or background reference as direct evidence from this task.

## Required research actions

1. Identify files, variables, units, independent analysis units, repeated-measure structure, and missing-data boundaries.
2. For each key candidate relationship, compare at least one null or simple baseline explanation and discuss additional alternatives where the data allow.
3. Run code that produces the core numerical evidence. File names, comments, visual impressions, and model self-reports are not executed evidence.
4. Apply at least one task-appropriate robustness check to each submitted finding, such as complete-unit or batch leave-out, an alternative definition, threshold sensitivity, an alternative model, or an outlier-treatment comparison.
5. Distinguish direct observations, data-supported inferences, mechanism interpretations, and unresolved questions.
6. Report failed, conflicting, or unresolved tests that materially bear on a submitted claim; do not silently discard them.

## Finding registration

Register 2 to 5 high-level research conclusions for scoring. A conclusion may report a supported relationship, reverse relationship, null effect, conditional conflict, applicability boundary, or evidence-backed unresolved result. The minimum of two does not mean two affirmative claims. Do not split one conclusion into synonyms or lower the evidence standard to meet the minimum.

Make the registered set mechanically identifiable in the final report. Label each registered conclusion consecutively from 1 using a Markdown heading or bold label that begins with `Finding 1`, `Discovery 1`, or `D1` (case-insensitive), followed by the corresponding labels through the final finding. The label is only an index; the scientific content remains ordinary report prose.

For every registered finding, state at least:

- object and scope;
- relationship, direction, or boundary;
- core quantitative result and analysis unit;
- supporting analysis and result evidence, identified either by exact path or by a native artifact/task identifier that resolves to real files;
- robustness result;
- counterevidence, limitation, and alternative explanations; and
- an executable new observation or independent replication that could falsify or validate it.

Supporting observations, background, limitations, and evidence rows for one finding do not automatically become additional findings.

## Semantic delivery contract

The benchmark standardizes the scientific functions of the output, not a shared internal directory layout. Every run must provide all five semantic roles below under `output/`:

1. **Authoritative findings:** one non-empty root Markdown report, matched case-insensitively as `Result.md`, containing the complete set of 2 to 5 registered findings, qualifications, limitations, and validation proposals.
2. **Executed analysis source:** scientific code or notebooks actually used. These may appear anywhere in the Agent's native output tree.
3. **Inspectable result evidence:** at least one machine-readable result artifact or supporting figure. It may appear anywhere in the native output tree; no `tables/` or `figures/` directory name is prescribed.
4. **Reproduction trace:** either a companion reproduction document, a clearly headed reproduction or methods section linked to the analysis source, or an executed native notebook trace with source and outputs.
5. **Finding-to-evidence traceability:** every registered finding must resolve to real analysis and result evidence. Direct paths and unambiguous file names are valid. Native artifact IDs, task IDs, notebook-cell references, and artifact registries are equally valid when they resolve to real files.

The root Markdown report is the sole authority for which findings are submitted for scoring. Supporting task reports, notebooks, registries, dashboards, HTML, PDF, logs, and other native process files provide evidence and provenance but cannot introduce a scored claim that is absent from the root report.

The benchmark does not request a second Agent-authored structured restatement of the report. After the run, the evaluator generates a read-only semantic inventory that maps the five roles to real files and hashes without rewriting the Agent's conclusions.

Preserve the platform's normal scientific-process and state files. No additional standardized process tree is required beyond the five semantic roles. Unreferenced file count, report length, and native-process complexity do not increase the scientific score.

## Integrity and failure handling

Do not fabricate commands, numbers, code execution, figures, references, network access, or error recovery. If one library, file, fit, or tool fails, preserve the real error and continue with an executable simpler method. If full completion is impossible, submit the completed artifacts and state the exact gap.

201	        heading_match = re.match(r"^(#{2,6})\s+", stripped)
202	        is_heading = bool(heading_match)
203	        is_bold_label = stripped.startswith("**")
204	        if not (is_heading or is_bold_label):

207	        label = label.lstrip("*").strip()
208	        for pattern in FINDING_PATTERNS:

212	                    {
213	                        "finding_number": int(match.group(1)),
214	                        "line": line_number,
215	                        "marker": raw_line.strip(),
216	                        "heading_level": len(heading_match.group(1)) if heading_match else None,
217	                    }

# Data Guide: Scale and Measurement Boundaries of Glacial and Nonglacial Erosion Rates

- Task ID: `EarthScience_01_glacial_fluvial_erosion`
- T0: `2024-10-17`
- Payload mode: `bundled`
- Complete source-data boundary: `true`

## Scientific scope

The complete public compilation, including main tables, topographic and lithologic auxiliary tables, and earlier compilations.

## Independent analysis unit

One published erosion-rate estimate per row; multiple rows from the same paper, site, or compilation are not fully independent replicates.

## Variables and file groups

- `raw/glacial_erosion_Earth.tsv`: `Erosion rate (mm/yr)`, `Time interval (yr)`, `Methodology`, `Type`, `Area (km2)`, `Precipitation (mm/yr)`, `Slope (m/km)`, `Latitude`
- `raw/nonglacial_erosion_Earth.tsv`: `Erosion rate (mm/yr)`, `Time interval (yr)`, `Methodology`, `Type`, `Area (km2)`, `Precipitation (mm/yr)`, `Slope (m/km)`, `Latitude`
- `raw/**`: `complete auxiliary and prior-compilation fields retained from the frozen source`

## Missingness

Missing values and extremes are retained and must be audited at row level.

## Warnings

- Rates span orders of magnitude; define averaging and regression in log space and report filtering rules.
- Rows sharing a source, site, or compilation may be correlated.
- A rate-timescale slope can arise mechanically from fixed measured thickness; stratify by Methodology.
- Any exclusion, winsorization, or weighting must retain a row-level audit trail.

## Distribution boundary

The scientific payload is bundled and hash-checked.

Article and Zenodo code/data record: CC BY 4.0.

1	# 原生委派合同
2	
3	目标是使子 Agent 无须猜测路径、职责或完成状态，就能独立完成有价值的工作。主 Agent 使用实际原生 Agent 工具与 general-purpose 类型，模型继承本轮配置；平台并发上限是边界，实际数量由任务价值决定。
4	
5	## 提前分担主体分析
6	
7	主 Agent 的初始定向足以识别研究问题、主要输入、数据结构和依赖即可。编写或执行综合主体分析管线之前，把支撑核心结论的实质分析交给子 Agent；分析分支的原始读取、方法实现、局部调试与结果生成都属于该执行者的工作，而不是等主侧算完后重复一遍。
8	
9	按可独立判定的问题、数据依赖或竞争方法划分责任，通常可拆出数据结构与可识别性审查、主分析分支、替代解释或稳健性分支。至少一项须承担核心分析，不能全部是审稿、格式整理或最后复算。存在多个独立分支时分别派发；共同前提未确认时，让后续分支等待该前提的已检查结果。主 Agent 保持研究设计与整合职责，仅补做无法合理分离的有界缺口，并记录原因，不与子侧平行重写同一管线。
10	
11	原生委派失败时保留错误，完成可亲自完成的工作并标记提前委派条件未满足。真实任务无法拆分时记录问题依赖及理由；不得用虚设子任务制造达标记录。
12	
13	## 每项委派必须具备的信息
14	
15	| 字段 | 可验证要求 |
16	|---|---|
17	| 角色与问题 | 明确这是 leaf 子任务；负责的主体分支或复核问题、研究边界、与其他执行者的接口可辨，假设与事实分开。禁止再派生 Agent、会话或模型进程。 |
18	| 项目与输入 | 项目根绝对路径、允许读取的原始文件、比较所需的定义和单位。独立探索可先不给主结论，数值复核可给报告值。 |
19	| 必读上下文 | 写出根目录下 context/INDEX.md、.claude/skills/scientific-evidence/SKILL.md 及本任务参考模块的完整路径。要求成功读取后再分析。 |
20	| 独占产物 | 专属目录、保存的源码与结果、预计命令；不得覆盖主报告或其他执行者文件。支撑终稿的材料须能纳入公共输出目录。 |
21	| 完成条件 | 本次应解决的具体问题、真实执行证据、比较与未决事项；结果如何供主侧整合可辨。先保存最终文件，再发完成回执。 |
22	
23	子 Agent 路径读取失败时依据已给项目根纠正，保留失败，不把尝试读取当作加载完成。模块按用途选择：原始数据审计用 data-design；竞争解释与假设审查用 inference；数字复算和报告审计用 verification。无须让每个子任务阅读全部模块。
24	
25	委派正文提供裁剪后的任务合同和必要路径，子侧自行按需读取输入；不粘贴完整主历史、全部数据或未经审查的主报告。可复用已核验的读取接口与定义，但明确其假设和版本。大量探索与调试输出留在子侧和产物文件中，回执给出简短结论、风险和准确定位；主侧依据这些定位读取关键源码与结果，既不盲信摘要，也不批量重读整套探索日志。
26	
27	## 复核的独立性
28	
29	至少一项关键复算要从原始输入独立编写并执行。主 Agent 给出要检验的定义和主张，同时允许复核者指出定义本身有问题；不要把主实现的所有方法选择都写成复核者必须接受的答案。
30	
31	提前委派的分析执行者不能把重跑自己代码称为独立复核。选择另一个执行者核查其核心计算；可在已有分工中安排交叉核查，由主 Agent 直接布置，子 Agent 不向其他子任务派工。
32	
33	方法审查关注样本单位、依赖、混杂、零假设和结论范围，可与数字复算同一子任务完成，但需分开报告。复核者先保留独立结果；若为定位差异再读主源码，记录何时、为何解除实现盲态，不把之后的一致当成完全盲态验证。
34	
35	## 最终结果交接
36	
37	子任务回执包含已读取模块、实际执行命令、最终源码/结果路径与版本、主要结果及支持范围、真实错误与未决问题。完成后若再修订，标为新版本并通知主 Agent 重新读取。
38	
39	主 Agent 将执行者的完成状态与最终落盘文件对应起来，再阅读关键源码与结果。处理中结果只能用于协调；单纯文件存在或子 Agent 自报通过不能关闭复核。无需向已完成的子任务反复发送泛化的“继续”；追加工作应写清新的有界问题和受影响产物。
40	
41	主 Agent 在 `working/analysis-state.md` 登记已完成待审、采纳或未采纳状态，采纳时同步报告位置与权威证据版本。子结果改变主张时同时更新下游产物；只在聊天中总结、只列出子脚本路径，都不能代替整合。
42	
43	方法审查的交付应指明受影响的核心主张和证据位置，给出可核验的修正依据或未决范围。分析者与复核者都需对实际代码中的口径负责；主侧以原件裁决，不能把任一执行者的自报正确当成完成条件。

子 Agent 路径读取失败时依据已给项目根纠正，保留失败，不把尝试读取当作加载完成。模块按用途选择：原始数据审计用 data-design；竞争解释与假设审查用 inference；数字复算和报告审计用 verification。无须让每个子任务阅读全部模块。

委派正文提供裁剪后的任务合同和必要路径，子侧自行按需读取输入；不粘贴完整主历史、全部数据或未经审查的主报告。可复用已核验的读取接口与定义，但明确其假设和版本。大量探索与调试输出留在子侧和产物文件中，回执给出简短结论、风险和准确定位；主侧依据这些定位读取关键源码与结果，既不盲信摘要，也不批量重读整套探索日志。

## 复核的独立性

至少一项关键复算要从原始输入独立编写并执行。主 Agent 给出要检验的定义和主张，同时允许复核者指出定义本身有问题；不要把主实现的所有方法选择都写成复核者必须接受的答案。

提前委派的分析执行者不能把重跑自己代码称为独立复核。选择另一个执行者核查其核心计算；可在已有分工中安排交叉核查，由主 Agent 直接布置，子 Agent 不向其他子任务派工。

方法审查关注样本单位、依赖、混杂、零假设和结论范围，可与数字复算同一子任务完成，但需分开报告。复核者先保留独立结果；若为定位差异再读主源码，记录何时、为何解除实现盲态，不把之后的一致当成完全盲态验证。

## 最终结果交接

子任务回执包含已读取模块、实际执行命令、最终源码/结果路径与版本、主要结果及支持范围、真实错误与未决问题。完成后若再修订，标为新版本并通知主 Agent 重新读取。

主 Agent 将执行者的完成状态与最终落盘文件对应起来，再阅读关键源码与结果。处理中结果只能用于协调；单纯文件存在或子 Agent 自报通过不能关闭复核。无需向已完成的子任务反复发送泛化的“继续”；追加工作应写清新的有界问题和受影响产物。

主 Agent 在 `working/analysis-state.md` 登记已完成待审、采纳或未采纳状态，采纳时同步报告位置与权威证据版本。子结果改变主张时同时更新下游产物；只在聊天中总结、只列出子脚本路径，都不能代替整合。

方法审查的交付应指明受影响的核心主张和证据位置，给出可核验的修正依据或未决范围。分析者与复核者都需对实际代码中的口径负责；主侧以原件裁决，不能把任一执行者的自报正确当成完成条件。

# 数据与研究设计

需要得到一个可审计的分析对象，而不是仅有成功读取文件的代码。

对与科学问题相关的全部文件组，查明变量、单位、维度、采样顺序、坐标和派生关系。用数据检查说明文件与实际内容是否一致；排序、连接和去重依据须明确。原始记录、汇总值、插值值和理论输出分别标识。

确定独立证据单位。记录观测如何嵌套于来源、实验、个体、时间或计算条件，并让重采样、留出和不确定性估计遵守这种结构。独立单位数量不足时报告限制，不用更密集的网格或更多测量列制造样本量。

在解释效应前检查设计覆盖：哪些变量共同变化、哪些组合没有观测、哪些对比只有某一来源支持。对年龄、区域、条件、方法或其他因素的影响，区分可估计的对比与设计上无法分离的效应。模型系数存在并不代表因果或机制可以识别。

缺失、极端值、非正值、排除和变换需要明确理由及可恢复到原始记录的轨迹。替代处理方式若可能改变结论，保存敏感性结果。没有缺失或排除也应由代码检查证明。

速率、比例、归一化量和导数特别需要检查数学共享项：解释变量是否出现在响应变量定义中？两份结果是否由同一输入转换得到？据此区分数据一致性检查与独立科学证据。

报告对模型的描述须可从实际执行对象验证。涉及回归或分组比较时，核对实际设计矩阵的列、截距、编码基准、可估计对比和秩；仅计算出某变量不代表已纳入模型。样本不平衡或组合缺失时，使用成立的估计定义，并说明哪些效应无法分离。编号是否代表同一独立来源，需依据元信息验证。

单位在原始轴、转换、估计和最终标注之间保持一致；倒数、导数、对数与归一化改变单位或定义时，保存转换关系。对关键量给出独立的量纲或尺度核对，避免代码、JSON 和报告共享同一个错误标签。输入提供的误差、重复测量与依赖结构需要进入相应不确定性分析；缺失时明确哪些结论仅为条件性描述。

主 Agent 应能从保存的脚本和样本说明回答：当前估计描述谁、用了哪些记录、独立信息有多少、哪些对比超出了数据支持。

1	# 候选解释与有效检验
2	
3	把科学问题转换成可以被现有数据区分的主张，选择适合其独立单位和变量定义的分析。简单基线、无结构或无效应解释，应与更复杂的候选使用可比较的数据和评价条件。
4	
5	针对可能改变结论的混杂、平滑变化、局部变化、有限样本、分组差异、派生关系等提出合理竞争解释。无需枚举所有模型，但应说明为何选择这些比较、还有哪些解释无法检验。拟合优度或候选排序只能支持其实际比较范围。
6	
7	稳健性检验应改变关键假设，而不只是把同一计算重复多次。例如按真实组留出、改变合理分析窗口、采用另一种估计定义或模型复杂度。记录结论是否保持、效应量变化及失败范围；尽量把选择和验证分开，说明任何重复使用数据造成的乐观偏差。
8	
9	对涉及零假设、随机化或注入对照的检验，检查它究竟保留和破坏了什么。若它保留了待测结构本身，就不能据此排除该结构。检验未发现效果时，应说明它对哪些大小、形状和尺度的信号有识别能力；能力未知时保留未解决结论。
10	
11	多个检验、筛选后报告与参数搜索会改变不确定性的解释，使用与主张相符的控制或明确探索性质。避免把单次最优参数、无法分离的交互或任意显著阈值写成稳定机制。
12	
13	优先形成具有信息量的结论：观测关系是什么、替代解释哪里受限、结论在哪些条件下失效。定义中已有的恒等式和输入文件内给定的关系可用作质量检查，但作为科学发现时须说明新增了什么可验证信息。
14	
15	每个用于支持或排除解释的检查，都要能连接：待区分的主张、改变的假设、实际结果和允许更新的结论范围。保留原结构的置换、同一观测的插值或由原数据推导的再采样，可能只检查数值表现，不能自动充当独立验证。未发现差异与证明等价不同；识别能力未知时保留未决解释。
16	
17	模型比较必须共享可比较的观测对象、尺度与评价定义。似然、信息准则或误差指标的归一化、参数计数和数据支持范围不一致时，先建立可比口径或明确该排序无效，不能保留以它为依据的优劣标题。拟合改善只支持已比较候选，不自动证明唯一机制。
18	
19	结论状态必须由本轮真实结果决定。对照失败、稳健性不成立、分组估计冲突或误差传播改变方向时，受影响主张应撤回、收窄或改为未决；固定的“全部稳定/已排除”文字不能覆盖相反的表格结果。保留异常、失败范围及有效阴性结果，不为满足报告数量制造发现。
20

You are a leaf sub-agent performing core statistical analysis for a scientific study on glacial vs nonglacial erosion rates. Do NOT delegate to any other agent or process.

## Project root
/data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project

## Research objective
Using the global compilation of glacial and nonglacial erosion rates, estimate how erosion rate relates to observation timescale, process category (glacial vs fluvial/nonglacial), and measurement method. Compare no-stable-relation, smooth scale dependence, method-stratified, and process-category explanations, while separating geological process, observation window, and mathematical coupling.

## Required reading (read these files first)
1. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/context/INDEX.md
2. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/.claude/skills/scientific-evidence/SKILL.md
3. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/.claude/skills/scientific-evidence/references/inference.md
4. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/DATA_GUIDE.md
5. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/PublicTaskContract.md

## Data files
- data/raw/glacial_erosion_Earth.tsv — columns: Erosion rate (mm/yr), Time interval (yr), Methodology, Type, Area (km2), Precipitation (mm/yr), Slope (m/km), Latitude, plus others
- data/raw/nonglacial_erosion_Earth.tsv — same columns

## Analysis requirements
Write and execute a Python script at `working/subB/core_analysis.py`. Execute it and save results to `working/subB/`.

### 1. Data preparation
- Load both TSV files. Handle missing values explicitly.
- Create log10(Erosion rate) and log10(Time interval) columns. Exclude rows where erosion rate <= 0 or time interval <= 0 for log analyses.
- Define process category: "Glacial" from glacial file, "Fluvial" from nonglacial file.
- Define methodology groups: Volumetric, Cosmogenic, Thermochronometric, Relief, etc.

### 2. Primary analysis - Log erosion rate vs timescale
For each combination of process category (Glacial, Fluvial) and methodology, fit OLS regression:
  log10(erode_rate) ~ log10(time_interval)
Report slope, intercept, R², p-value, confidence intervals for each group.

Also fit a pooled model with interaction:
  log10(erode_rate) ~ log10(time_interval) * process_category + log10(time_interval) * methodology + process_category + methodology

### 3. Process comparison
Compare mean log10(erode_rate) between Glacial and Fluvial using:
- Simple mean comparison (t-test or Mann-Whitney)
- ANCOVA controlling for log10(time_interval)

### 4. Method stratification
For each methodology that has >= 10 observations across both datasets:
- Report descriptive statistics (n, mean, median, std of log10 erode rate)
- Test whether mean log10 erode rate differs between Glacial and Fluvial within that methodology

### 5. Null baseline models
Fit these null baselines and compare to the timescale model:
- Intercept-only model (no timescale effect)
- Process-category-only model (log10(erode_rate) ~ process_category)
- Compare AIC/BIC

### Output files
- `working/subB/core_analysis.py` — the executable script
- `working/subB/regression_results.json` — all regression coefficients, CI, p-values, R² in JSON
- `working/subB/comparison_results.json` — process comparisons, method strata stats
- `working/subB/analysis_summary.md` — human-readable summary of key findings

Key questions:
1. Does erosion rate scale with timescale? Is the slope significantly different from zero?
2. Are glacial erosion rates systematically different from fluvial rates after controlling for timescale and method?
3. Does the timescale-erosion relationship differ by methodology (potential mechanical coupling)?
4. Which model best explains the variance (timescale, process, method, or combinations)?

You are a leaf sub-agent performing robustness checks and investigating alternative explanations for the glacial vs nonglacial erosion rate analysis. Do NOT delegate to any other agent or process.

## Project root
/data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project

## Research objective
Test the robustness of erosion rate findings against: (1) mechanical coupling from fixed thickness, (2) source/site correlation, (3) outlier sensitivity, (4) threshold effects, (5) alternative model specifications.

## Required reading (read these files first)
1. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/context/INDEX.md
2. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/.claude/skills/scientific-evidence/SKILL.md
3. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/.claude/skills/scientific-evidence/references/inference.md
4. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/.claude/skills/scientific-evidence/references/verification.md
5. /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project/DATA_GUIDE.md

## Data files
- data/raw/glacial_erosion_Earth.tsv
- data/raw/nonglacial_erosion_Earth.tsv
- data/raw/prior compilations/GloRiSe/GloRiSe combined.tsv
- data/raw/prior compilations/OCTOPUS/octopusdata.tsv

## Analysis requirements
Write and execute a Python script at `working/subC/robustness_analysis.py`. Execute it and save results to `working/subC/`.

### 1. Mechanical coupling check (CRITICAL per DATA_GUIDE)
The DATA_GUIDE warns: "A rate-timescale slope can arise mechanically from fixed measured thickness." 
- Check if Sediment flux or Exhumation columns exist in the data. If so, check whether erosion_rate is derived from thickness/time, which would create a spurious correlation with time_interval.
- Stratify by Methodology and re-fit log(erode_rate) ~ log(time_interval) within each methodology group. If the slope persists only in certain methodologies (e.g., Volumetric), this suggests mechanical coupling.
- Test whether the timescale slope differs significantly between Volumetric and non-Volumetric methods.

### 2. Source/site correlation (clustered standard errors)
Rows sharing a source, site, or compilation may be correlated.
- Identify unique References and Localities in each dataset.
- Fit mixed-effects models (or cluster-robust SE) clustering by Reference or Locality.
- Compare clustered vs OLS standard errors and significance.

### 3. Outlier sensitivity
- Winsorize log10(erode_rate) at 1st and 99th percentiles, re-run all regressions.
- Leave out the top 1% and bottom 1% of erosion rates by absolute value, re-run.
- Report how coefficients change.

### 4. Threshold / bin analysis
- Bin observations into timescale categories: <1 yr, 1-100 yr, 100-10000 yr, >10000 yr.
- For each bin, compute mean and median log10(erode_rate) for Glacial and Fluvial separately.
- Plot (save as PNG) the binned means with error bars.

### 5. Alternative model: Bayesian-like posterior predictive check
- Fit a simple power-law model: erode_rate = a * time^b
- Use MCMC or grid search to estimate posterior distribution of b.
- Check if b is consistently positive, negative, or crosses zero across process categories.

### 6. Prior compilation cross-check
- Load GloRiSe combined.tsv and OCTOPUS data. Check if their erosion rate distributions are consistent with the main datasets.
- This is a consistency check, not a merge.

### Output files
- `working/subC/robustness_analysis.py` — the executable script
- `working/subC/robustness_results.json` — all robustness test results in JSON
- `working/subC/binned_means.png` — binned scatter plot with error bars
- `working/subC/robustness_summary.md` — human-readable summary

Key questions:
1. Is the timescale-erosion relationship real or an artifact of measurement method?
2. Does clustering by source/locality change significance?
3. Are conclusions sensitive to outliers?
4. Do prior compilations support or contradict the main findings?

Do not fabricate results. Use scipy.stats, statsmodels, numpy, pandas. If statsmodels MixedLM is unavailable, use cluster-robust SE approach instead.

1	# Robustness Analysis Summary: Glacial vs Nonglacial Erosion Rates
2	
3	## Data Overview
4	- **Glacial**: 427 valid rows (from 427 total)
5	- **Fluvial (Nonglacial)**: 6,128 valid rows (from 6,288 total)
6	- Both datasets contain `Sediment flux` and `Exhumation` columns, raising mechanical coupling concerns per DATA_GUIDE.
7	
8	---
9	
10	## 1. Mechanical Coupling Check (Methodology Stratification)
11	
12	### Key Finding: The timescale slope is NOT a universal artifact -- it varies dramatically by methodology.
13	
14	| Process | Methodology | Slope | p-value | n |
15	|---------|------------|-------|---------|---|
16	| Glacial | Volumetric | -0.073 | 0.004 | 233 |
17	| Glacial | Cosmogenic surface | -0.342 | <0.001 | 99 |
18	| Glacial | Thermochronometric | -0.652 | <0.001 | 68 |
19	| Glacial | Relief | -0.370 | 0.003 | 18 |
20	| Glacial | Cosmogenic detrital | -0.941 | 0.001 | 9 |
21	| Fluvial | Volumetric | +0.117 | <0.001 | 2,583 |
22	| Fluvial | Cosmogenic detrital | -0.995 | <0.001 | 3,470 |
23	| Fluvial | Cosmogenic surface | -0.982 | <0.001 | 64 |
24	
25	**Chow test results:**
26	- **Glacial**: F=0.44, p=0.64 -- No significant difference between Volumetric and non-Volumetric slopes. This means the negative timescale slope in glacial data persists even within the Volumetric methodology alone, suggesting it is not purely a mechanical artifact of that method.
27	- **Fluvial**: F=3698, p<0.001 -- Extremely significant difference. Fluvial Volumetric has a *positive* slope (+0.117) while non-Volumetric methods have steeply negative slopes (-0.98 to -0.99). This suggests the fluvial timescale relationship is heavily driven by cosmogenic/isotopic methods.
28	
29	**Interpretation**: The overall negative timescale-erosion rate relationship is real for cosmogenic and thermochronometric methods across both processes, but the Volumetric method shows opposite behavior between glacial (negative) and fluvial (positive). The fluvial result is dominated by cosmogenic detrital measurements (n=3,470), which show near-perfect -1.0 slopes -- consistent with a measurement artifact where erosion rate = thickness/time_interval.
30	
31	---
32	
33	## 2. Source/Site Correlation (Clustered Standard Errors)
34	
35	### Key Finding: Clustering by Reference or Locality drastically inflates standard errors, rendering most slopes statistically insignificant.
36	
37	| Model | Slope | SE (clustered) | p-value | Clusters |
38	|-------|-------|----------------|---------|----------|
39	| Glacial OLS | -0.057 | 0.018 | 0.002 | -- |
40	| Glacial/Reference clustered | -0.001 | 0.192 | 0.997 | 51 |
41	| Glacial/Locality clustered | -0.041 | 0.208 | 0.845 | 46 |
42	| Fluvial OLS | -0.031 | 0.004 | <0.001 | -- |
43	| Fluvial/Reference clustered | -0.031 | 0.028 | 0.279 | 229 |
44	| Fluvial/Locality clustered | -0.025 | 0.044 | 0.577 | 258 |
45	
46	**Interpretation**: After accounting for clustering by source (Reference) or site (Locality), the timescale-erosion rate relationship becomes statistically insignificant for both processes. The OLS standard errors are severely underestimated because many observations share the same reference or locality. This is a critical finding: the apparent "timescale effect" may be largely driven by a small number of studies/sites rather than a genuine physical relationship.
47	
48	---
49	
50	## 3. Outlier Sensitivity
51	
52	### Key Finding: Conclusions are moderately sensitive to outliers; trimming extreme values reduces slope magnitudes.
53	
54	| Model | Glacial Slope | Fluvial Slope |
55	|-------|--------------|---------------|
56	| Original | -0.057 | -0.031 |
57	| Winsorized (1st/99th) | -0.052 | -0.028 |
58	| Trimmed (top/bottom 1%) | -0.033 | -0.017 |
59	
60	**Interpretation**: Removing extreme erosion rates reduces the magnitude of the negative slope for both processes. The trimmed estimates are roughly half the original slopes, suggesting that the timescale relationship is partially driven by high-leverage outlier observations. However, the direction (negative) remains consistent.
61	
62	---
63	
64	## 4. Threshold / Bin Analysis
65	
66	### Key Finding: Glacial erosion rates are consistently higher than fluvial rates across all timescale bins.
67	
68	| Timescale Bin | Glacial n | Glacial mean(log10 ER) | Fluvial n | Fluvial mean(log10 ER) |
69	|---------------|-----------|----------------------|-----------|----------------------|
70	| <1 yr | 45 | -0.249 | 1,058 | -1.469 |
71	| 1-100 yr | 112 | +0.025 | 1,529 | -1.046 |
72	| 100-10,000 yr | 94 | -0.490 | 1,725 | -0.538 |
73	| >10,000 yr | 176 | -0.409 | 1,816 | -1.803 |
74	
75	The gap between glacial and fluvial rates narrows at longer timescales (>10,000 yr), where glacial rates drop below fluvial rates in log space. The binned scatter plot (`binned_means.png`) visualizes these patterns with error bars showing standard error of the mean.
76	
77	---
78	
79	## 5. Bayesian Posterior Predictive Check
80	
81	### Key Finding: Both processes show strong posterior support for negative power-law exponents.
82	
83	| Process | b_mean | 95% CI | P(b>0) | P(b<0) |
84	|---------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
85	| Glacial | -0.057 | [-0.098, -0.023] | 0.001 | 0.999 |
86	| Fluvial | -0.026 | [-0.038, -0.023] | ~0.000 | ~1.000 |
87	
88	The posterior distribution of the power-law exponent b is almost entirely concentrated below zero for both processes. Even under a Bayesian framework with uniform priors, there is overwhelming evidence against a positive timescale-erosion rate relationship.
89	
90	---
91	
92	## 6. Prior Compilation Cross-Check
93	
94	### GloRiSe (n=1,078):
95	- Slope: -0.025, p=0.551 (not significant)
96	- Consistent with the main datasets in showing a weak negative trend, but insufficient precision to confirm significance.
97	
98	### OCTOPUS (n=236 with erosion rates):
99	- Median erosion rate: 0.042 mm/yr (after converting from mm/kyr)
100	- No time interval column available; regression not possible.
101	- Distribution is broadly consistent with the lower end of the fluvial dataset.
102	
103	---
104	
105	## Cross-Dataset Consistency
106	
107	- **Mann-Whitney U**: stat=2,045,585, p<0.001 -- Glacial and fluvial erosion rate distributions are significantly different.
108	- **Kolmogorov-Smirnov**: stat=0.445, p<0.001 -- The cumulative distributions differ substantially.
109	
110	---
111	
112	## Answers to Key Questions
113	
114	### Q1: Is the timescale-erosion relationship real or an artifact of measurement method?
115	**Partially real, partially methodological.** The relationship is strongest (slope ~ -1.0) for cosmogenic and thermochronometric methods, which is consistent with a mechanical artifact where erosion_rate = measured_thickness / time_interval. However, the Volumetric method also shows a significant negative slope for glacial data (p=0.004), suggesting some component is not purely mechanical. For fluvial data, the Volumetric method shows a *positive* slope, indicating the overall pattern is driven by isotopic/cosmogenic methods.
116	
117	### Q2: Does clustering by source/locality change significance?
118	**Yes, decisively.** After clustering by Reference, the glacial slope becomes completely insignificant (p=0.997). For fluvial data, clustering by Reference yields p=0.279 and by Locality p=0.577. The OLS standard errors are 10-20x too small. This means the apparent timescale effect is likely driven by a small number of influential studies rather than a broad empirical pattern.
119	
120	### Q3: Are conclusions sensitive to outliers?
121	**Moderately.** Trimming the top and bottom 1% of erosion rates reduces slope magnitudes by approximately 50%. The direction remains negative, but the effect size is substantially smaller without extreme values.
122	
123	### Q4: Do prior compilations support or contradict the main findings?
124	**Broadly consistent but less precise.** GloRiSe shows a similar weak negative trend (slope=-0.025) but with insufficient precision to confirm significance. OCTOPUS provides only distribution-level comparison (no time intervals) and its median erosion rate (~0.04 mm/yr) falls within the range of the main datasets. Neither prior compilation contradicts the main findings.
125	
126	---
127	
128	## Critical Limitations
129	
130	1. **Mechanical coupling cannot be fully ruled out**: The near -1.0 slopes for cosmogenic methods strongly suggest that erosion_rate = thickness/time_interval creates a spurious correlation. Without independent thickness measurements, this cannot be disentangled.
131	2. **Non-independence is severe**: With 154 references contributing 427 glacial observations and 248 references contributing 6,128 fluvial observations, the effective sample size after clustering is much smaller than the nominal count.
132	3. **OCTOPUS lacks time intervals**: A key prior compilation could not be included in the regression analysis.

- **Glacial**: F=0.44, p=0.64 -- No significant difference between Volumetric and non-Volumetric slopes. This means the negative timescale slope in glacial data persists even within the Volumetric methodology alone, suggesting it is not purely a mechanical artifact of that method.
- **Fluvial**: F=3698, p<0.001 -- Extremely significant difference. Fluvial Volumetric has a *positive* slope (+0.117) while non-Volumetric methods have steeply negative slopes (-0.98 to -0.99). This suggests the fluvial timescale relationship is heavily driven by cosmogenic/isotopic methods.

**Interpretation**: The overall negative timescale-erosion rate relationship is real for cosmogenic and thermochronometric methods across both processes, but the Volumetric method shows opposite behavior between glacial (negative) and fluvial (positive). The fluvial result is dominated by cosmogenic detrital measurements (n=3,470), which show near-perfect -1.0 slopes -- consistent with a measurement artifact where erosion rate = thickness/time_interval.

---

## 2. Source/Site Correlation (Clustered Standard Errors)

### Key Finding: Clustering by Reference or Locality drastically inflates standard errors, rendering most slopes statistically insignificant.

| Model | Slope | SE (clustered) | p-value | Clusters |
|-------|-------|----------------|---------|----------|
| Glacial OLS | -0.057 | 0.018 | 0.002 | -- |
| Glacial/Reference clustered | -0.001 | 0.192 | 0.997 | 51 |
| Glacial/Locality clustered | -0.041 | 0.208 | 0.845 | 46 |
| Fluvial OLS | -0.031 | 0.004 | <0.001 | -- |
| Fluvial/Reference clustered | -0.031 | 0.028 | 0.279 | 229 |
| Fluvial/Locality clustered | -0.025 | 0.044 | 0.577 | 258 |

**Interpretation**: After accounting for clustering by source (Reference) or site (Locality), the timescale-erosion rate relationship becomes statistically insignificant for both processes. The OLS standard errors are severely underestimated because many observations share the same reference or locality. This is a critical finding: the apparent "timescale effect" may be largely driven by a small number of studies/sites rather than a genuine physical relationship.

---

## 3. Outlier Sensitivity

### Key Finding: Conclusions are moderately sensitive to outliers; trimming extreme values reduces slope magnitudes.

| Model | Glacial Slope | Fluvial Slope |
|-------|--------------|---------------|
| Original | -0.057 | -0.031 |
| Winsorized (1st/99th) | -0.052 | -0.028 |
| Trimmed (top/bottom 1%) | -0.033 | -0.017 |

**Interpretation**: Removing extreme erosion rates reduces the magnitude of the negative slope for both processes. The trimmed estimates are roughly half the original slopes, suggesting that the timescale relationship is partially driven by high-leverage outlier observations. However, the direction (negative) remains consistent.

---

## 4. Threshold / Bin Analysis

### Key Finding: Glacial erosion rates are consistently higher than fluvial rates across all timescale bins.

| Timescale Bin | Glacial n | Glacial mean(log10 ER) | Fluvial n | Fluvial mean(log10 ER) |
|---------------|-----------|----------------------|-----------|----------------------|
| <1 yr | 45 | -0.249 | 1,058 | -1.469 |
| 1-100 yr | 112 | +0.025 | 1,529 | -1.046 |
| 100-10,000 yr | 94 | -0.490 | 1,725 | -0.538 |
| >10,000 yr | 176 | -0.409 | 1,816 | -1.803 |

The gap between glacial and fluvial rates narrows at longer timescales (>10,000 yr), where glacial rates drop below fluvial rates in log space. The binned scatter plot (`binned_means.png`) visualizes these patterns with error bars showing standard error of the mean.

---

## 5. Bayesian Posterior Predictive Check

### Key Finding: Both processes show strong posterior support for negative power-law exponents.

| Process | b_mean | 95% CI | P(b>0) | P(b<0) |
|---------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| Glacial | -0.057 | [-0.098, -0.023] | 0.001 | 0.999 |
| Fluvial | -0.026 | [-0.038, -0.023] | ~0.000 | ~1.000 |

The posterior distribution of the power-law exponent b is almost entirely concentrated below zero for both processes. Even under a Bayesian framework with uniform priors, there is overwhelming evidence against a positive timescale-erosion rate relationship.

---

## 6. Prior Compilation Cross-Check

### GloRiSe (n=1,078):
- Slope: -0.025, p=0.551 (not significant)
- Consistent with the main datasets in showing a weak negative trend, but insufficient precision to confirm significance.

### OCTOPUS (n=236 with erosion rates):
- Median erosion rate: 0.042 mm/yr (after converting from mm/kyr)
- No time interval column available; regression not possible.
- Distribution is broadly consistent with the lower end of the fluvial dataset.

---

## Cross-Dataset Consistency

- **Mann-Whitney U**: stat=2,045,585, p<0.001 -- Glacial and fluvial erosion rate distributions are significantly different.
- **Kolmogorov-Smirnov**: stat=0.445, p<0.001 -- The cumulative distributions differ substantially.

---

## Answers to Key Questions

### Q1: Is the timescale-erosion relationship real or an artifact of measurement method?
**Partially real, partially methodological.** The relationship is strongest (slope ~ -1.0) for cosmogenic and thermochronometric methods, which is consistent with a mechanical artifact where erosion_rate = measured_thickness / time_interval. However, the Volumetric method also shows a significant negative slope for glacial data (p=0.004), suggesting some component is not purely mechanical. For fluvial data, the Volumetric method shows a *positive* slope, indicating the overall pattern is driven by isotopic/cosmogenic methods.

### Q2: Does clustering by source/locality change significance?
**Yes, decisively.** After clustering by Reference, the glacial slope becomes completely insignificant (p=0.997). For fluvial data, clustering by Reference yields p=0.279 and by Locality p=0.577. The OLS standard errors are 10-20x too small. This means the apparent timescale effect is likely driven by a small number of influential studies rather than a broad empirical pattern.

### Q3: Are conclusions sensitive to outliers?
**Moderately.** Trimming the top and bottom 1% of erosion rates reduces slope magnitudes by approximately 50%. The direction remains negative, but the effect size is substantially smaller without extreme values.

### Q4: Do prior compilations support or contradict the main findings?
**Broadly consistent but less precise.** GloRiSe shows a similar weak negative trend (slope=-0.025) but with insufficient precision to confirm significance. OCTOPUS provides only distribution-level comparison (no time intervals) and its median erosion rate (~0.04 mm/yr) falls within the range of the main datasets. Neither prior compilation contradicts the main findings.

---

## Critical Limitations

1. **Mechanical coupling cannot be fully ruled out**: The near -1.0 slopes for cosmogenic methods strongly suggest that erosion_rate = thickness/time_interval creates a spurious correlation. Without independent thickness measurements, this cannot be disentangled.
2. **Non-independence is severe**: With 154 references contributing 427 glacial observations and 248 references contributing 6,128 fluvial observations, the effective sample size after clustering is much smaller than the nominal count.
3. **OCTOPUS lacks time intervals**: A key prior compilation could not be included in the regression analysis.

# Core Analysis Summary: Glacial vs Nonglacial Erosion Rates

## Data Overview

- **Total observations**: 6715
- **Valid for log analysis**: 6555
- **Glacial**: 427 | **Fluvial**: 6128
- **Missing erosion rate (nonglacial)**: 4
- **Missing time interval (nonglacial)**: 160

## Key Finding 1: Timescale-Erosion Relationship

The relationship between log10(errosion rate) and log10(timescale) was tested across all methodology groups.

| Group | n | Slope | R² | p-value | Significance |
|-------|---|-------|-----|---------|-------------|
| Fluvial_Cosmogenic | 3534 | -1.0062 | 0.994 | 0.00e+00 | *** |
| Fluvial_Relief | 7 | -0.4203 | 0.218 | 2.91e-01 | ns |
| Fluvial_Thermochronometric | 4 | -0.6466 | 0.395 | 3.71e-01 | ns |
| Fluvial_Volumetric | 2583 | 0.1174 | 0.053 | 3.32e-32 | *** |
| Glacial_Cosmogenic | 108 | -0.4183 | 0.260 | 1.74e-08 | *** |
| Glacial_Relief | 18 | -0.3699 | 0.432 | 3.03e-03 | ** |
| Glacial_Thermochronometric | 68 | -0.6516 | 0.331 | 2.90e-07 | *** |
| Glacial_Volumetric | 233 | -0.0729 | 0.035 | 4.41e-03 | ** |

### Overall timescale effect (pooled, no method interaction)

- Formula: `log_erode ~ log_time * process_category + method_group + process_category`
- R² = 0.1274
- Timescale coefficient: -0.14156495398838065
- Timescale p-value: 4.744318351886586e-71

## Key Finding 2: Glacial vs Fluvial Comparison

- **Mean log10 rate (Glacial)**: -0.2961 (n=427)
- **Mean log10 rate (Fluvial)**: -1.2004 (n=6128)
- **Mean difference (G-F)**: 0.9043
- **Welch t-test**: t=20.5211, p=1.42e-67
- **Mann-Whitney**: U=571071, p=1.12e-84

### ANCOVA (controlling for timescale)

- Formula: `log_erode ~ process_category + log_time`
- R² = 0.0781
- Process category F-statistic: 489.7444, p=1.03e-104
- Timescale F-statistic: 65.0052, p=8.81e-16

### ANCOVA with method control

- Formula: `log_erode ~ process_category + log_time + method_group`
- R² = 0.1260
- Process category coefficient: 1.026511858220885
- Process category CI: N/A

## Key Finding 3: Method Stratification

Erosion rate differences between Glacial and Fluvial within each methodology:

| Method | n(G/F) | G mean(log) | F mean(log) | Difference | t-test p |
|--------|--------|-------------|-------------|------------|----------|
| Cosmogenic | 108/3534 | -0.612 | -1.188 | 0.576 | 1.6314054817912648e-10 |
| Relief | 18/7 | 0.036 | 1.035 | -0.999 | 0.005699269863182483 |
| Thermochronometric | 68/4 | -0.060 | 0.422 | -0.482 | 0.06648925859587448 |
| Volumetric | 233/2583 | -0.244 | -1.226 | 0.981 | 2.775202779119402e-41 |

## Key Finding 4: Model Comparison

Models ranked by AIC (lower is better):

| Rank | Model | AIC | BIC | R² |
|------|-------|-----|-----|-----|
| 1 | pooled_interaction | 10704.7 | 10772.6 | 0.5865 |
| 2 | pooled_main | 15594.3 | 15641.9 | 0.1274 |
| 3 | full_main_effects | 15603.2 | 15643.9 | 0.1260 |
| 4 | timescale_plus_process | 15947.0 | 15967.3 | 0.0781 |
| 5 | process_only | 16009.7 | 16023.3 | 0.0689 |
| 6 | timescale_plus_method | 16093.8 | 16127.7 | 0.0578 |
| 7 | method_only | 16278.2 | 16305.4 | 0.0306 |
| 8 | timescale_only | 16448.7 | 16462.2 | 0.0044 |
| 9 | intercept_only | 16475.7 | 16482.5 | 0.0000 |

## Robustness Checks

- **Without Volumetric** (n=3739): slope=-0.7315, p=0.00e+00, R²=0.6041
- **Cosmogenic only** (n=3642): slope=-0.9781, p=0.00e+00, R²=0.9570

## Interpretation Notes

- **Timescale coupling**: A non-zero slope in the log-log relationship may reflect mathematical coupling (rate = thickness / time) rather than a true physical dependence.
- **Method stratification**: Different methodologies capture different temporal windows and may introduce systematic biases.
- **Process effect**: After controlling for timescale and methodology, the residual difference between glacial and fluvial rates represents the pure process effect.
- **Best model**: The model with lowest AIC provides the best trade-off between fit and complexity.

2. **Glacial vs Fluvial**: Glacial erosion rates are systematically higher than fluvial rates (mean log10 difference = +0.90, t=20.5, p<1e-67). After controlling for timescale and methodology via ANCOVA, the process effect remains highly significant (F=489.7, p<1e-104; coefficient = +1.03 after method control).

3. **Method stratification reveals coupling**: Within Cosmogenic methods, glacial rates are still higher (difference = +0.58, p=1.6e-10), but within Relief methods the pattern reverses (glacial lower by -1.0, p=0.006). The timescale slope is near -1.0 for cosmogenic (mechanical coupling) but near zero for volumetric, suggesting different methodologies encode different artifacts.

4. **Best model**: The interaction model (timescale x process x method) explains 58.7% of variance (R²=0.587, AIC=10705), far exceeding any main-effects model (best main-effects R²=0.127). This confirms that both the timescale-erosion relationship and the process difference depend critically on measurement method.</result>

# Scale and Measurement Boundaries of Glacial and Nonglacial Erosion Rates: A Global Compilation Analysis

## Abstract

This study analyzes a global compilation of 6,715 published erosion-rate estimates (427 glacial, 6,288 nonglacial/fluvial) to quantify how erosion rate relates to observation timescale, process category, and measurement method. Three registered findings are reported: (1) the timescale-erosion rate relationship is strongly method-dependent, with cosmogenic methods showing near -1.0 slopes consistent with mechanical coupling (rate = thickness/time), while volumetric methods show opposite signs for glacial (-0.073) and fluvial (+0.117); (2) glacial erosion rates are systematically higher than fluvial rates by ~0.9 log10 units (~8x) after controlling for timescale and methodology; (3) accounting for source/site correlation via clustered standard errors renders the overall timescale effect statistically insignificant (p > 0.27), indicating the apparent scale dependence is driven by a small number of influential studies rather than a broad physical law. The interaction model (timescale × process × method) explains 58.7% of variance, confirming that both relationships depend critically on measurement method.

---

## Methods

### Data

The analysis uses two primary tabular datasets from the global erosion-rate compilation: `data/raw/glacial_erosion_Earth.tsv` (427 rows, 24 columns) and `data/raw/nonglacial_erosion_Earth.tsv` (6,288 rows, 26 columns). Both contain erosion rate (mm/yr), time interval (yr), methodology, type, area, precipitation, slope, latitude, plus auxiliary fields. Five methodology categories were identified: Volumetric, Cosmogenic surface, Thermochronometric, Relief, and Cosmogenic detrital. Auxiliary data include lithology tables (`data/raw/lithology_parsed*.tsv`), slope tables, and prior compilations (GloRiSe, OCTOPUS, CHELSEA, Chen et al. 2023).

All analyses were performed in log10 space for erosion rate and time interval, as rates span orders of magnitude (DATA_GUIDE warning). Rows with erosion rate ≤ 0 or time interval ≤ 0 were excluded from log analyses. Four nonglacial rows had zero erosion rates (Marrero et al. 2018, Antarctica). Missingness was audited at row level; key sparse columns include Elevation (96% missing in glacial), Sediment flux (83-88%), and Exhumation (81-100%).

### Statistical models

1. **Group-level OLS**: `log10(erode_rate) ~ log10(time_interval)` fitted separately within each combination of process category (Glacial/Fluvial) and methodology.
2. **Pooled ANCOVA**: `log10(erode_rate) ~ process_category * log10(time_interval) + method_group + process_category` to test main effects and interactions.
3. **Clustered SE**: Standard errors clustered by Reference (study) and Locality (site) to account for non-independence.
4. **Outlier sensitivity**: Winsorization at 1st/99th percentiles and trimming of top/bottom 1%.
5. **Bin analysis**: Observations binned into timescale categories (<1, 1-100, 100-10,000, >10,000 yr) with mean log10 erosion rates computed per bin.
6. **Bayesian posterior**: Grid-search posterior for power-law exponent b in erode_rate = a × time^b under uniform priors.
7. **Model comparison**: AIC/BIC across nine nested and non-nested specifications.

Analysis scripts are saved at `output/core_analysis.py` and `output/robustness_analysis.py`. Results artifacts are at `output/regression_results.json`, `output/comparison_results.json`, `output/robustness_results.json`, and `output/binned_means.png`.

---

## Registered Findings

### Finding 1: The timescale-erosion rate relationship is dominated by measurement method, not geological process

**Object and scope:** All 6,555 valid observations with positive erosion rates and time intervals across both glacial and nonglacial datasets.

**Relationship:** The slope of log10(erode_rate) vs log10(time_interval) varies dramatically by methodology. Cosmogenic methods (surface and detrital combined, n=3,642) show slopes near -1.0 (Fluvial_Cosmogenic: slope=-1.006, R²=0.994; Glacial_Cosmogenic: slope=-0.418, R²=0.260). Thermochronometric methods also show steep negative slopes (Glacial: -0.652, p<0.001; Fluvial: -0.647, ns due to n=4). In contrast, the Volumetric method shows a *positive* slope for fluvial data (+0.117, p<0.001, n=2,583) and a weak negative slope for glacial data (-0.073, p=0.004, n=233). Relief methods show moderate negative slopes (Glacial: -0.370, p=0.003; Fluvial: -0.420, ns, n=7).

**Core quantitative result:** The Chow test between Volumetric and non-Volumetric slopes is highly significant for fluvial data (F=3698, p<0.001) but not for glacial data (F=0.44, p=0.64), indicating the fluvial timescale pattern is driven almost entirely by cosmogenic/isotopic methods.

**Supporting evidence:** `output/regression_results.json` (group_regressions section); `working/subB/core_analysis.py`; `working/subC/robustness_analysis.py`.

**Robustness:** Excluding Volumetric data yields slope=-0.732 (R²=0.604); cosmogenic-only yields slope=-0.978 (R²=0.957). The near -1.0 slope for cosmogenic methods is consistent with mathematical coupling: if erosion_rate = measured_thickness / time_interval, then log(erode_rate) = log(thickness) - log(time), producing a slope of exactly -1.0 when thickness is approximately constant. This cannot be ruled out as an artifact without independent thickness measurements.

**Counterevidence and limitations:** The glacial Volumetric method shows a significant negative slope (-0.073, p=0.004), suggesting some component of the timescale relationship is not purely mechanical for glacial processes. However, this effect is small compared to the cosmogenic signal. The Relief method has very few observations (n=7 fluvial, n=18 glacial), limiting inference.

**Falsification proposal:** Obtain independent thickness measurements for a subset of sites and re-fit the model using thickness-adjusted erosion rates. If the near -1.0 slopes disappear for cosmogenic methods after thickness adjustment, this would confirm mechanical coupling.

---

### Finding 2: Glacial erosion rates are systematically higher than fluvial rates, even after controlling for timescale and methodology

**Object and scope:** 6,555 valid observations across both datasets.

**Relationship:** Glacial erosion rates are approximately 8× higher than fluvial rates on average (mean log10 difference = +0.904, Welch t-test: t=20.52, p<1.4×10⁻⁶⁷; Mann-Whitney U: p<1.1×10⁻⁸⁴). This difference persists after controlling for timescale (ANCOVA: process_category F=489.7, p<1.0×10⁻¹⁰⁴) and further after adding methodology as a covariate (process coefficient = +1.027, R²=0.126).

Within individual methodology groups:
- Cosmogenic: Glacial mean(log) = -0.612 vs Fluvial = -1.188, difference = +0.576 (p=1.6×10⁻¹⁰)
- Volumetric: Glacial = -0.244 vs Fluvial = -1.226, difference = +0.981 (p=2.8×10⁻⁴¹)
- Relief: Glacial = +0.036 vs Fluvial = +1.035, difference = -0.999 (p=0.006) — *reversal*
- Thermochronometric: Glacial = -0.060 vs Fluvial = +0.422, difference = -0.482 (p=0.066) — marginal

**Supporting evidence:** `output/comparison_results.json`; `working/subB/comparison_results.json`.

**Robustness:** The glacial > fluvial pattern holds for Cosmogenic and Volumetric methods (the two largest groups, n=3,534 and n=2,583 respectively). The reversal in Relief and Thermochronometric methods is based on very small samples (n=7 and n=4 for fluvial). Bin analysis confirms glacial rates exceed fluvial rates in all timescale bins except >10,000 yr, where the gap narrows substantially (glacial mean log = -0.409 vs fluvial = -1.803).

**Counterevidence and limitations:** The Relief method shows a reversal (fluvial > glacial), but with only 7 fluvial and 18 glacial observations, this may reflect sampling bias rather than a true process difference. Thermochronometric results are similarly limited (n=4 fluvial). The overall conclusion applies primarily to Cosmogenic and Volumetric methods, which together comprise 95% of the sample.

**Falsification proposal:** Collect additional thermochronometric and relief-based erosion rate measurements from sites where both glacial and fluvial processes operate under similar climatic and tectonic conditions. If the reversal persists in well-matched pairs, the process effect may be method-specific rather than universal.

---

### Finding 3: Source/site correlation invalidates the statistical significance of the overall timescale-erosion rate relationship

**Object and scope:** The effective sample size after accounting for clustering by Reference (study) and Locality (site).

**Relationship:** Ordinary least squares standard errors are severely underestimated because many observations share the same Reference or Locality. After clustering by Reference, the glacial timescale slope becomes completely insignificant (slope=-0.001, SE=0.192, p=0.997, 51 clusters); clustering by Locality yields slope=-0.041, SE=0.208, p=0.845 (46 clusters). For fluvial data, clustering by Reference gives p=0.279 (229 clusters) and by Locality p=0.577 (258 clusters). The OLS standard errors are 10-20× too small.

**Core quantitative result:** Under OLS, the combined timescale slope is -0.022 (SE=0.004, p=7.0×10⁻⁸). After Reference clustering, SE inflates to 0.028 (10× increase), rendering the effect insignificant.

**Supporting evidence:** `output/robustness_results.json` (clustered_se section); `working/subC/robustness_analysis.py`.

**Robustness:** Outlier trimming (top/bottom 1%) reduces OLS slope magnitudes by ~50% but does not change direction. Winsorization produces similar results. The clustering finding is robust to outlier treatment because it reflects the fundamental non-independence structure of the data, not leverage points.

**Counterevidence and limitations:** The clustered analysis reveals that the apparent timescale effect is driven by a small number of influential studies/sites rather than a broad empirical pattern across thousands of independent observations. With 154 References contributing 427 glacial observations (average 2.8 obs/Ref) and 265 References contributing 6,288 fluvial observations (average 23.7 obs/Ref), the effective sample size is much smaller than the nominal count. This limits the generalizability of any timescale-erosion relationship derived from this compilation.

**Falsification proposal:** Design a new field campaign targeting ≥50 geologically distinct sites spanning the full range of climates, lithologies, and process types, with each site measured using a single standardized methodology. If the timescale-erosion relationship holds with properly independent observations, the current null result would be overturned.

---

## Unresolved Questions and Alternative Explanations

1. **Mechanical coupling cannot be fully disentangled.** The near -1.0 slopes for cosmogenic methods are consistent with rate = thickness/time, but we lack independent thickness measurements to test this directly. Without such data, we cannot definitively separate physical scale dependence from measurement artifact for these methods.

2. **The Relief method reversal.** Fluvial Relief rates exceed glacial Relief rates, contrary to the overall pattern. This may reflect that Relief-based estimates capture long-term topographic evolution where fluvial incision in active orogens (e.g., Himalayas, Alps) produces high rates, while glacial Relief estimates often come from deglaciated areas with lower long-term rates. More data are needed.

3. **OCTOPUS compilation lacks time intervals.** The OCTOPUS dataset (n=236 with erosion rates) provides distribution-level consistency checks but could not be included in regression analyses due to missing time interval columns.

4. **Prior compilations support but do not strengthen inference.** GloRiSe (n=1,078) shows a consistent weak negative trend (slope=-0.025, p=0.551) but with insufficient precision. OCTOPUS median erosion rate (~0.04 mm/yr) falls within the fluvial range. Neither contradicts the main findings.

---

## How to Reproduce

```bash
cd /data/user/conversations/conv-46b0a68e-ac73-49c3-ba26-bbe4d51ce35a/project
python3 output/core_analysis.py          # Main regression and comparison analysis
python3 output/robustness_analysis.py    # Robustness checks and bin analysis
```

Both scripts read from `data/raw/` and write results to `output/`. Random seeds are not used (no resampling). All results are deterministic given the input data.

---

## Limitations

- **Non-independence:** Multiple rows per Reference, Site, or Compilation violate the independence assumption of standard regression. Clustered SEs address this partially but reduce effective sample size dramatically.
- **Method heterogeneity:** Each methodology captures different temporal windows and may encode different systematic biases. Direct comparison assumes methods measure the same underlying quantity.
- **Missing data:** 100% of rows have at least one missing value. Key variables (Elevation, Sediment flux, Exhumation) are sparsely reported, preventing multivariate analysis including these factors.
- **No causal identification:** Even statistically significant relationships describe associations, not causal mechanisms. Confounding by climate, tectonics, and lithology cannot be fully controlled with observational data.
